interactions.summary: A student reads Beatrice's lines distinguishing the matter of a vow from its formal compact and warning that some vowed matter cannot be substituted away.

Jiang glosses the passage through Hannah Arendt, arguing that promise-making is one of the two fundamentally human actions because it binds people to one another and to a jointly imagined future, then quizzes the class on the second action.
Students guess at lying or sacrifice, but Jiang steers the answer toward apology and forgiveness, saying the other action that expresses humanity is forgiving broken promises and mistakes.

Jiang turns the Arendt frame back to Dante: a good society empowers both promise-making and forgiveness, and Piccarda's vow to God matters because some promises are too weighty for straightforward compensation.

claims.claim: The Dante passage distinguishes between the matter of a vow and its formal compact, and it warns that some vowed matter has so much weight that no substitute can balance it out.
Jiang says making promises is a fundamentally human action because a promise binds one person to another and binds both of them to an imagined future.
Jiang argues that forgiving others for broken promises or mistakes is the other fundamentally human action that, alongside promise-making, expresses and uplifts humanity.
Jiang says a good, just, moral, even divine society is one where people are empowered both to make promises and to forgive one another.
Jiang frames Piccarda's vow to God as a promise so valuable that the usual logic of compensation or substitution becomes unstable, which is why Beatrice is about to complicate the issue.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang makes promise-making a future-binding power: when two people promise, they are not only attaching themselves to each other but imagining a future together.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It carries the packet beyond textual commentary into Jiang's social ontology, which will matter for both the public read and later lens work on promise, agency, and political order.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang names the twin acts that make us most human: to make promises and to forgive each other for breaking them.
signature_moments.source_phrase: to make promises and to forgive each other
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's memorable compression and the conceptual hinge for his reading of vows, political order, and mercy.

signature_moments.moment: A just society, for Jiang, is not defined first by rules but by whether people are empowered to promise and empowered to forgive.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It preserves the strong normative jump from classroom discussion to political theology instead of flattening the packet into a generic ethics summary.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The binding form of a vow, distinguished from the concrete matter pledged in the vow itself.
The actual thing promised or sacrificed in a vow, which Jiang's Dante passage treats as carrying its own irreducible weight.
Jiang's Arendt-inflected description of a uniquely human action that binds people into a shared future.
The paired human action that repairs broken promises and mistakes, completing the social world that promises begin.

chronology_notes.note: After the prior packet's anti-reductionist debate, this 2026-06-16 packet abruptly relocates the seminar into vows, Arendt on promises and forgiveness, and the moral architecture of society, setting up Piccarda as a test case for when sacred promises collide with lived complexity.
